summary: Fixes a problem in how pseudowire endpoints negotiate use of the control word. It updates RFC 4447 and RFC 6073 by adding the Label Request message, which resolves the issue when a provider edge changes its preference from not preferred to preferred. It is a standards-track specification. It was replaced by RFC 8077.

eli5.summary: Two friends agree on a secret handshake, but one changes their mind and the other does not notice. This memo adds a way to ask again so both end up using the same handshake.

questions: how to update rfc 4447 control word
label request message for control word
subtitle: Fixes a negotiation deadlock when provider edges change their preference for control words.

tldr.problem: RFC 4447 defines pseudowire control-word negotiation, but it has a flaw: if a provider edge changes its preference from NOT PREFERRED to PREFERRED, the negotiation fails and both endpoints remain stuck with control words disabled.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6723 adds a Label Request message that either endpoint can send to force renegotiation of the control-word preference, resolving the deadlock without breaking backward compatibility.
tldr.outcome: Pseudowire control-word preference can now be dynamically renegotiated. RFC 8077 later replaced this update with a cleaner approach.

today: RFC 6723 was superseded by RFC 8077, which provides a cleaner and more comprehensive update to pseudowire control-word handling. RFC 6723 remains relevant for deployments that have not yet updated to RFC 8077.

sections.title: Pseudowires and Control Words
sections.content:
A pseudowire is an MPLS mechanism for emulating a point-to-point connection between two provider edge routers. Instead of sending traffic over a direct link, the routers encapsulate it into an MPLS tunnel. Each pseudowire can optionally use a control word—a small header added to each frame to carry flags and sequence information that help with packet ordering and loss detection.

RFC 4447 lets each provider edge configure its preference: "I prefer to use the control word" or "I prefer not to use it." The two endpoints negotiate during session setup: if both prefer control words, they use them; otherwise, they do not. This works well—unless something changes after setup.
sections.eli5: A pseudowire is like a virtual tunnel between two routers. They can agree to add a small control label to each packet (the control word) to track ordering and catch lost packets. RFC 4447 says they talk it over at the start and agree on whether to use it.

sections.title: The Negotiation Deadlock
sections.content:
The problem arises when a provider edge router changes its local configuration after the pseudowire is already set up. Suppose PE1 initially prefers control words and PE2 does not. During negotiation, PE1 respects PE2's preference and sends a Label Mapping message with the control-word bit (C-bit) set to 0, meaning "do not use control word." Both routers are now happy with this decision.

Later, PE2 is reconfigured to prefer control words. PE2 deletes and reconfigures the pseudowire with the new preference. RFC 4447 says that after PE2 sends a Label Withdraw, it must examine the previously received Label Mapping from PE1—which still says C-bit equals 0. When PE2 responds with its own Label Mapping, it also sets C-bit to 0, following the negotiation rules. Even though both routers now prefer control words, they remain locked into "do not use control word." This is a deadlock.
sections.eli5: When one router changes its mind but the other router remembers the old agreement, they get stuck. They both prefer the control word now, but neither one asks the other to reconsider, so they stay with the old decision.

sections.title: The Label Request Message
sections.content:
RFC 6723 fixes this by adding a Label Request message. When a provider edge detects that it has changed its preference from NOT PREFERRED to PREFERRED, and it previously received a Label Mapping with C-bit set to 0, it triggers renegotiation: send a Label Release message, then a Label Withdraw (if needed), and finally a Label Request message.

The Label Request is already defined in RFC 5036; the update simply specifies that when received, the peer PE resets its locally configured control-word preference and sends a fresh Label Mapping message reflecting its current preference. The requesting PE then applies the standard RFC 4447 negotiation rules to the new pair of preferences. This forces both endpoints to reconsider and settle on the correct outcome.
sections.eli5: The new Label Request message is like saying "Let us talk about this again." Each router forgets the old agreement, says what it prefers right now, and they negotiate again from scratch.

sections.title: Multi-Segment Pseudowires
sections.content:
A multi-segment pseudowire stitches together multiple single-segment pseudowires across intermediate switching provider edges. RFC 6073 defines how segment stitching works. RFC 6723 extends the Label Request renegotiation to multi-segment topologies by giving switching PE routers a passive role: when an S-PE receives a Label Request, it forwards a matching Label Request to the adjacent PE on the other side, effectively relaying the renegotiation request through the entire path.

This ensures that all switching PE routers in the path also update their preferences consistently. The order matters: when an S-PE receives a Label Withdraw before a Label Request, it processes the withdraw first, sends the corresponding Label Release, and then handles the Label Request in the next step. Backward compatibility is maintained because the Label Request and Label Release messages are already defined in RFC 5036 and RFC 4447; routers updated to RFC 6723 simply handle them in a new context.
sections.eli5: When the tunnel passes through multiple routers, each one in the middle relays the renegotiation request onward so everybody agrees at the same time.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 6723 introduces no new security risks. The security model is unchanged from RFC 4447 and RFC 6073: Label Withdraw, Label Release, and Label Request messages are protected by the same LDP authentication mechanisms, and the renegotiation does not bypass any existing checks.

The update is fully backward compatible. A provider edge that has not implemented RFC 6723 will simply ignore the Label Request message (it treats it as unknown) or gracefully handle it according to RFC 5036. In single-segment scenarios, a newer PE can renegotiate with an older PE that does not support this update, because the older PE simply responds to the Label Request with its then-current preference, allowing the newer PE to make the right choice. Operators can deploy RFC 6723 incrementally without disrupting existing pseudowires.
sections.eli5: The renegotiation uses the same secure handshakes as before. Routers that do not support this update will still work with routers that do, so operators do not need to upgrade everything at once.
